# GTA Cyber

> GTA Cyber is the cybersecurity community of practice within Global Tech Advocates. It is not a regional
> chapter or a vertical business line. It is a cross-cutting group that draws on
> cybersecurity practitioners already inside GTA networks worldwide and makes that
> expertise available across the whole organisation. Volunteer-led, independent and
> not-for-profit.

Parent organisation: Global Tech Advocates, https://www.globaltechadvocates.org/
Website: https://gta-cyber.org/
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/gta-cyber
Contact: info@gta-cyber.org

## The model

GTA Cyber is a community of practice rather than a vertical silo: a cross-cutting
group of subject matter experts who sit across business units, divisions and locations
instead of inside any one of them. Members keep their existing Global Tech Advocates
network membership and their day jobs. The community sits across those networks, so a
security question raised in one city can be answered by a practitioner in another.
People join because of the craft they practise rather than where they are based.

Global Tech Advocates has more than 40,000 business leaders, experts and investors
across 42 or more networks worldwide.

## Focus areas

- **Orchestrated digital governance**: the gap between discovering a digital estate and
  actually governing it. One picture that security, GRC, legal and brand can act on at
  once, with an owner, a deadline and an audit trail for every asset and finding.
- **The convergence of AI and cybersecurity**: two distinct problems routinely discussed
  as one. Securing AI systems (model supply chain, prompt handling, data leakage, agency)
  and using AI in security (whether output can be trusted enough to act on).
- **Data sovereignty, viewed through a security lens**: beyond jurisdiction and contract
  terms, where data physically sits including backups, logs and unmapped fourth parties;
  which keys exist and who holds them; what technically happens when a provider is
  compelled to disclose.
- **The grey digital divide**: the philanthropic strand. Essential services went digital
  by default, making digital access a precondition for banking, healthcare and government.
  Older people are the group most likely to be excluded and among the most targeted by
  fraud once online. Exclusion and victimisation reinforce each other; the remedy is
  inclusion, not warning people off the internet.

## How the community works

Two standing mechanisms, distinct from the subjects above:

- **Practitioner exchange**: a standing forum for security people across GTA networks
  to share what works, what failed and what is coming. Chatham House rules by default.
- **Expertise on call**: when another GTA group, a member company or a policy
  conversation needs a security view, the community routes it to someone qualified.

## What the community does not do

Certify or accredit anyone. Compete with its own members for work. Run an incident
response service. Publish threat intelligence as a product.

## Events

Monthly practitioner calls, quarterly deep-dive roundtables, policy response sessions
convened when a consultation has a real deadline, and security strands contributed to
events run by other GTA groups.

## Funding and sponsorship

Volunteer-led and sponsor-funded, in the same model as the wider Global Tech Advocates
organisation. Nobody draws a salary; sponsorship pays for programme delivery.

Klarvant (https://klarvant.com/) is the founding title sponsor.

Sponsorship tiers: title sponsor (held by Klarvant), programme partner, in-kind
supporter. Sponsorship does not buy the membership list, editorial control, or
guaranteed speaking slots. Guidance published by the community is vendor-neutral,
including in categories where sponsors compete.

## Security

Vulnerability disclosure policy: https://gta-cyber.org/security-policy
security.txt: https://gta-cyber.org/.well-known/security.txt
Security contact: security@gta-cyber.org
No bug bounty programme; no payment is offered for reports.
